newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn tax talks fail, despite Buba warnings.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn tax talks fail, despite Buba warnings.

text.p: Talks aimed at reforming German tax systems collapsed in failure on Wednesday, despite warnings from the Bundesbank and independent analysts that such reforms were an essential step to cutting vast jobless queues.

The talks between the German coalition and Social Democrat (SPD) opposition on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's proposed package of 30 billion marks ($17.5 billion) in tax cuts, broke off after just an hour with each side blaming the other.
"The SPD was not able to agree to our planned tax cuts and pensions reforms," Waigel told reporters. "The SPD wants to cut occupational insurance charges by just redistributing wealth."
SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine hit back that the government had flatly rejected its call to link tax reforms to cutting the jobs costs in a bid to fight high German unemployment.

The collapse opens the way for a bruising parliamentary battle between the lower house, controlled by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition and the SPD-ruled second chamber, which could run into the 1998 general election campaign.
Independent analysts were not surprised by the outcome, but warned that investors would now be more wary of German assets.
Economists said the failure would add to financial market concerns that Kohl and Waigel face a fierce fight every inch of the way to make Germany's tax and pensions system more flexible.
"This will make things very difficult for the government if they want to push through austerity measures this year," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London.
The failure to achieve a breakthrough in the talks comes at a critical time, when Germany like most other European nations, is cranking up its motors for the final dash to monetary union.

Two official forecasts released on Wednesday gave varying assessments of Bonn's chances of coming anywhere close to its aim of a 2.9 percent deficit compared to gross domestic product this year, just below a three percent limit set for EMU entry.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said it expected Germany's budget deficit to shrink to 3.3 percent of gross domestic product this year from 3.8 percent in 1996.
The European Commission, in a forecast some analysts believed was politically-motivated, said Germany would hit the nail on the head with a 3.0 percent deficit this year.
It was record employment data in January which originally triggered now persistent fears that the extra budget burdens could undermine efforts to cut its budget deficits.

The Bundesbank reinforced these concerns in its 1996 annual report, released on Wednesday, warning that Germany should make extra efforts to rein in its budget deficit as unforeseen events could otherwise endanger its spending efforts.

"It can also not be ruled out that further unexpected burdens on the budget may arise in the course of the year, whether on the income side or on particular types of expenditure...efforts are needed to achieve further savings."

The central bank, in common with independent economists, also warned in its report that although German economic growth looked set to pick up this year that in itself would have little impact on Bonn's top problem, the weak labour market.

"Even if a clear economic recovery in the course of the year should put an end to the downtrend in employment levels and replaces it with an uptrend it is not likely that a strong fall in unemployment will result," it said.
A Reuter poll of economists drew similar conclusions.
Analysts polled at 27 banks said the German economy would pick up steam in 1997 and 1998 as companies sold more goods abroad but that unemployment, now at 11.2 percent, would come down only slowly.
They predicted growth in GDP of 2.2 percent in 1997 on average and of 2.7 percent in 1998.
Key German interest rates were seen remaining steady for the rest of 1997, but monetary conditions were expected to start to tighten at the turn of the year. ($ = 1.713 German Marks)
